  • Recovery agents, who have been working in the recovery area for a while and wish to acquire a deeper understanding of the internal functioning of banks and banking

What is the career potential after doing this course?

  • You can work in a full-service corporate law firm. Corporate law firms have two major departments for which you will be especially trained - project finance and banking and finance. Young lawyers struggle to understand the industry and therefore face challenges in performing everyday tasks. They also struggle to understand the big picture and commercials behind a large deal. In fact, even after a few years of experience, their understanding of the banking and finance industry and the legal work required is piecemeal. This course provides a systematic understanding of the industry and the skills required to perform specific legal tasks.
  • You can work as an in-house counsel in a bank or an NBFC. Due to the high volume of regulation, banks and financial companies have larger in-house legal teams than other companies. 
  • You will also acquire the skill sets to work as an in-house counsel of a large corporate group. In-house counsels of a large corporate group (Indian or global) need to be well-versed in banking and finance laws to be able to assist the group entities with obtaining finance for their regular business needs and with project finance, if the company is in the infrastructure sector. 
  • You can work as an in-house counsel of a fintech startup. The fintech space is witnessing rapid innovation post demonetization, and the COVID-19 lockdown has further accelerated this shift. As an example, Sachin Bansal is reported to have invested USD 450 million of the USD 1 bn exit amount he received from Walmart into his new investment firm Navi Technologies, which is making investments into the fintech space. We will continue to see fintech businesses rapidly scale up in the coming months and years. These fintech startups are in need of lawyers to perform a variety of regulatory, structuring and compliance-related work. They are also capable of rapidly scaling up, which is why this is a very important area for lawyers. As a lawyer who is well-versed in banking and finance laws, you will find yourself in a unique position to work for fintech startups, either as an independent lawyer/ freelancer or as an in-house counsel, as per your preference. You can also build an independent consultancy practice to advise fintech startups on different aspects.  
  • Independent lawyers and even in-house lawyers can help startups in availing benefits of various schemes initiated by the government to provide loans and benefits to SMEs. Most startups are in need of finance but do not know how to obtain it owing to the heavy paperwork involved. The government has initiated several schemes to provide different types of secured and unsecured loans to SMEs. A lawyer’s work in this area relates to identification of a relevant scheme, assisting through the application process which can be fairly complex and in advising entrepreneurs/founders about the commercial implications of the terms. Lawyers who do not understand the unique regulatory framework for the banking sector and lending and security documentation cannot advise startups in this area. 
  • If you are a litigator, you can be eligible to apply for openings to be on the panel of a private or public sector bank. Banks maintain a panel of litigators for enforcement-related matters for different forums and jurisdictions. Being on the panel offers you tremendous reputational benefits, enhances credibility in the opinion of clients, a stable volume of work and significant face-time before the court to build your credibility as an arguing counsel. You can continue to work on independent matters as well, as long as there is no conflict. 
  • Litigators can also represent corporate clients and their borrowers in connection with loan documentation work or enforcement-related matters at different forums such as the Debt Recovery Tribunal or the National Company Law Tribunal. As a litigator, you can represent borrowers or promoters who have provided guarantees against enforcement actions initiated by the bank in respect of defaults.

What will you learn?

  • You will learn the basic guidelines for drafting including how to structure and arrange your drafts while maintaining the flow and keeping the recipient in mind;
  • You will learn in-depth about the construction and different parts of a contract and understand the importance of each part as well as how to draft these clauses for different types of contracts relevant to the banking sector;
  • You will learn precisely what you need to do to ensure that your contract is enforceable, including the stamping, notarization, attestation, apostille etc.
  • You will learn negotiation techniques that can be used for the purpose of arriving at the desired solution with the lawyers of the opposite party;
  • You will learn which are the different types of financing facilities provided by the banks including long term and short term i.e. working capital facilities to enable a client to determine which would be the most appropriate or if you are in the in-house legal department of a bank, to review the product from the point of view of applicable regulations. 
  • You will also learn the various regulations applicable to banks in order to be able to determine their role and the boundaries within which they should operate for the purpose of various transactions such as lending, foreign direct investment, guarantees etc.
  • You will get a complete overview of the various recovery mechanisms which can be deployed by the banks such as securitisation, approaching the Debt Recovery Tribunal, initiating insolvency under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, filing and learn how to select the appropriate recovery mechanism for different types of borrowers.
  • In addition to the above, you will also learn about how fintech entities operate as well as the regulations applicable to the fintech entities such as Phone Pe, Udaan etc.

Specific Learning Objectives

  • Learn how any contract is drafted and the different parts of contracts, the relevance of each of the different types of clauses and how these can be drafted to benefit your client;
  • Learn how contracts should be reviewed and how you can identify what exactly in the clauses needs to be altered to suit your requirements;
  • Learn how to redline contracts received from the other party to the transaction;
  • Learn negotiation skills, which can help you to turn things to your advantage not only in contract-related negotiations but practically any and every business transaction that you may be a part of;
  • Learn which clauses of contracts are introductory, which are operative and which are boilerplate;
  • Learn precisely what conditions precedent, conditions subsequent, and completion clauses are and how these are relevant;
  • Learn about obligations and payment related clauses, different ways in which these can be drafted and the pitfalls in drafting these;
  • Learn what breach and enforcement related clauses are and the best way to draft these;
  • Learn precisely what legal requirements would be applicable to your specific contracts, such as stamping, registration, notarization, attestation and apostille.
  • Learn how contracts are executed and how to secure the correct authorisation for the execution of contracts;
  • Learn how to draft emails to external consultants and also how to present your findings to your seniors in banking set up;
  • Learn about different types of standard financing facilities offered by the banks and agreements entered into for such facilities;
  • Learn about what working capital facilities are and learn what fund based and non-fund based facilities are;
  • Learn about the various ways in which security is provided to the banks and the transaction documents which are required to be entered into in order to provide and perfect the security;
  • Learn what contractual comforts are and how these work;
  • Learn how Indian banks can be involved in external commercial borrowings and how external commercial borrowings work;
  • Learn about which clauses are specifically used in lending contracts and how these are drafted as well as implications of such clauses;
  • Learn what internal authorisations a borrower requires in order to ensure that availing the loan does not result in violating the Companies Act, 2013, the borrower’s constitution documents or other restrictions;
  • Learn how to draft clauses of syndicate loan agreements;
  • Learn about which regulations apply to banks and NBFCs and also about the specific directions of RBI on banking activities;
  • Learn about what the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 encompasses and how this knowledge is relevant for bankers;
  • Learn how foreign direct investment in companies work and learn what role Authorised Dealer banks play in it;
  • Learn about how overseas direct investment is made and what role Authorised Dealer banks play in it;
  • Learn how guarantees, letters of credit and standby letters of credit work in relation to import-export transactions;
  • Learn exactly how you can stay updated and on top of the many and varied regulations governing the BFSI sector;
  • Learn why the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) was needed and how it compares to other recovery-related mechanisms such as SARFAESI and RDBA;
  • Learn important concepts of IBC such as debt, financial debt and different types of creditors;
  • Learn about how insolvency can be initiated as a financial creditor and how the admission of the application works;
  • Learn about the extent of applicability of the moratorium upon admission of the insolvency application;
  • Learn about the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) and what exactly they are supposed to do;
  • Learn about how the Committee of Creditors is formed, what it is supposed to achieve and how it takes decisions;
  • Learn about how claims are submitted and what to do when these are rejected by the RP;
  • Learn how to initiate proceedings against the personal guarantors to corporate debtors and the pros and cons of filing insolvency claims against the company vis a vis those against the personal guarantors;
  • Learn about how an information memorandum is prepared, and an expression of interest is drafted;
  • Learn about who can and cannot become a resolution applicant;
  • Learn how resolution plans are drafted and what are the strategic consideration in drafting these;
  • Learn about the avoidable transactions and the lookback period on such avoidable transactions;
  • Learn about how the liquidation process works in the event that the NCLT does not approve the resolution plan;
  • Learn about how exactly the security can be enforced under the SARFAESI Act;
  • Learn how to draft demand and possession notices under SARFAESI as well as replies to demand notices;
  • Learn how to draft and review a Section 19 application by the bank under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993;
  • Learn how to draft a notice of dishonour of cheque and a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881;
  • Learn how to deal with complaints against banks under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019;
  • Learn how summary suits can be filed by banks and NBFCs to enforce retail loans;
  • Learn about how share and debenture pledges can be enforced;
  • Learn about how loans can be converted into equity shares;
  • Learn about the different methods of debt restructuring and how these work;
  • Learn about who recovery agents are, how to become a recovery agent and what work recovery agents do;
  • Learn and understand how to rescue finance or interim finance works and what are the risks of using interim finance in terms of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016;
  • Learn about what legal issues impact payment gateways, mobile banking and other payment systems;
  • Learn about how e-wallets and payment instruments work and their convertibility into cash;
  • Learn about how fintech entities use artificial intelligence and machine learning and how this use is regulated/facilitated by the regulators.

Introduction to Legal Drafting

Legal drafting is an important skill for lawyers - it involves learning how to draft various kinds of petitions to be filed in court, drafting contracts for clients, preparation of legal opinions or ‘legal memos’ (not moot court memos). These skills enable a lawyer to perform different kinds of billable work for clients and provide them value. 

These skills are highly valuable, but they are either not taught or taught in a very limited manner in law school. 

Although we have courses focussing on different areas of law, ranging from criminal litigation, civil litigation, contract drafting, business laws for in-house counsels, arbitration, NCLT Litigation, M&A, etc., over the past few years, thousands of learners have asked us for an introductory drafting course which enables them to get started with the practical side of the law.  

We have decided to launch this course, keeping in mind such requests. 

Legal drafting is crucial for any lawyer to perform client work effectively. As you gain more expertise, you may realize that drafting skills for different forums and different areas of law will differ. 

For example, petitions before a criminal court will be different from petitions before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) or from arbitration petitions. Similarly, a shareholders agreement will be very different from an employment agreement. 

However, basic legal drafting skills and practice is crucial for performing any kind of client work. When one starts learning, it is important to have a broad foundation. At this stage, it does not matter if you are not sure about which area of law you want to focus on and specialize in. 

What do these drafting skills comprise?  

Learning how to draft a handful of contracts, civil and criminal petitions. This will enable you to have a preliminary sense of how to provide a service to a client. 

These drafting skills and practice will enable you to build confidence and feel equipped to understand and handle a variety of tasks assigned to junior lawyers. 

Later, if you want to learn about any specific kind of technical work, you can acquire specialized skills relevant to that area of practice.

How long will it take to learn these introductory skills? 

With our unique methodology, we are going to bet that you can learn them in 1-month.

Please scroll down - there is more for you.

You might know of some senior practitioners in your network who are very knowledgeable and talented but who are unable to build their clients. They are not able to enjoy the fruits of their knowledge because not enough people know about their expertise. 

Do you know why? They have not created a portfolio of work that is relevant and discoverable by their target audience.

We do not want you to face the risk of a similar fate.    
 
For this reason, article-writing skills are very important in today’s economy. You should have the ability to build a portfolio of expert-level articles in an area of your choice. Further, these articles should engage and be of interest to a reader, even if he or she is not a lawyer. For example, the reader could be a business owner, a working professional or manager, an individual who needs a lawyer or even a potential recruiter. 

We are clear that those who develop their article writing skills and create a published portfolio of work will enjoy a huge professional advantage in today’s world. Clients frequently search for young lawyers online, and the COVID-19 lockdown has drastically accelerated this shift. 

How can you start on this journey? The journey begins when you write one article in a time-bound manner and send it for publication. 

What would it take for you to learn these skills?

Approximately 2 hours of study per day at your own time and 1.5 hours of online classes with us.

We have identified a coaching framework for the same, and we will walk you through the journey of writing an article and sending it for publication, right from the point of identification of a topic to its completion. 

Guess what? All this can happen in a few months. Read on to find out more.

In fact, other professionals such as Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries, etc. and others who advise clients on different aspects of secretarial and accounting issues can also benefit from learning basic drafting skills.

We recommend that you should have completed your Higher Secondary / Class XII from a recognized Board / University. If any student is unable to attempt the test or facing any issues, can mail us at support@lawsikho.com 

Requirements of the online test may vary as per the course. We suggest you read the test details on the course page to learn more.

The online MCQ is executed on the Learning Management System. You do not have to go to any special centres to give the test or exam. You can attempt the test by logging on to the online Learning Management System from your home or anywhere you wish. We recommend using a computer while giving these tests, as mobile phones are unreliable for giving tests. 

Students should finish the MCQ test within the stipulated time in one sitting. 

Please visit the course page to know MCQ test fees and guidelines.

We are recreating the experience of working in a law firm or in-house legal department, and we found that this is the kind of training that works best. Live classes will relate to the week’s assignments. You can read the modules from module 1, but we advise you to follow the courses according to where the assignments take you. By the end of the year, you would have covered all the syllabus and retained everything.

If it feels complicated and challenging midway, do not worry. The course is designed like this. You need to stick to it, hold on for dear life and ride along as you ride a roller coaster. Our responsibility is that you are satisfied and get all the results that you were promised by the end. If you are not, you can hold us responsible. But please, please trust the course design and stick to it until the course gets over.

What is the course methodology?

  • Audiolingual method - Using this method, a learner will be able to listen and speak much before reading or writing. It ensures that the session isn’t only focussed on textual understanding, but also on comprehending the set data. 
  • Oral and situational language teaching - This is based on a structural view of language. Speech, structures and focus on a set of basic vocabulary items are seen as the basis of language teaching. An analysis of English and a classification of its prominent grammatical structures into sentence patterns. It ensures that learners internalise grammar rules. 
  • Grammar translation - the transition from controlled structures to the freer practice of structures, and from oral use of sentence patterns to automatic use in speech, reading, and writing. 
  • Task-based language teaching
  • Extremely interactive 
  • Immersive method
  • Language and content amalgamated and taught through various CLIL methodologies (Content and Language Integrated Learning) : 
  • BILD - Bilingual integration of languages and discipline.
  • LAC - Language across the curriculum.
  • EMI - English as a medium of instruction.
  • FLIP - Foreign language immersion programme.
  • Focus on assimilation and application.
  • Task-based explanation of concepts in order to ensure the thresholds are being met. 
  • Weekly charts will be given and effective implementation of the same will be done.
  • Weekly questionnaires will be shared, to check the understanding of the pupil. 
  • A stipulated time will be allotted at the end of each class to ensure that the doubts/questions are being cleared in each session

Join Master Access - Grow your practice rapidly by getting into new and exciting practice areas and learning new skills

 

Are you an independent practitioner or small law firm owner?
Do you earn around INR 1-2 lakhs per month or more from your law practice?
Are you running a small law firm and looking to get to the next level of growth?
Are you interested in building a law firm or a very profitable solo law practice with tens of lakhs of revenue per month?
You may then want to read on.

Myths That Need Not Stop You

  • I need grey hair to succeed as a lawyer. 
  • I need to be born into an elite legal family to succeed in the profession. 
  • I should not specialize early in my career. 
  • By specializing, I will lose clients and it will be hard to manage. 
  • Business development is solicitation and therefore illegal. 
  • If we follow the footsteps of successful lawyers of the previous generation, we will succeed. 
  • Successful lawyers don’t need any management/ customer service/ technology/ marketing/ administration to run our practice profitably. 
  • It is better to practice in the Supreme Court or High Court rather than tribunals or lower courts. 
  • I must charge less than big law firm partners to get work from a client. 
  • Big clients will prefer to go to big law firms only. 
  • I have to pay my juniors less. It would take a long time to train and onboard junior lawyers. 
  • I live in a small city or town - there is no work here and an absence of good opportunities. The legal profession is unfair. Seniors don’t pay or train, or invest in their juniors because juniors will leave. 
  • The expectation of clients or seniors is very high. 
  • The market is bad - we can’t do anything. 

If you are a law firm founder or an independent practitioner, answer the following questions truthfully (to yourself)

Don’t worry even if you answer quite a few of these questions in the affirmative. These are not real problems - the real problem is somewhere else and these can be fixed quite easily. 

But for now, just go through these questions and statements and see if anything resonates. 

 

  • Do you struggle to find new clients at times?
  • Do you feel that some clients don’t value your expertise? 
  • Do you find clients at times asking for specialized or customized services that you do not provide?
  • Do you struggle with clients driving your prices down because competitors are ready to undercut? 
  • Do some clients underestimate your ability to deliver results, or question your experience? 
  • Do you find it difficult to charge and justify higher prices for your services?
  • Do you feel confident in competing with more experienced lawyers? 
  • Do you want to identify new practice areas where you can deliver high-value services but not sure how to go about it? 
  • Do you find it hard to chase big mandates because of a lack of bandwidth, experience and an effective team? 
  • Are you worried about stagnation in your practice, while your batchmates or juniors get promoted and earn more?
  • Do you ever worry about being caught unprepared in a client meeting or in the courtroom by judges for not being on point? 
  • Are you concerned that lawyers with less capability are doing better than you because they are better at promoting themselves? 
  • Are you concerned about failing to build a brand name over time?
  • Do you often complain about not having any free time for your friends and family? Are you overworked and stressed?
  • Do you feel dissatisfied at the end of your day and wonder if you should just accept a job? 

 

If your hard work is not paying off, you may be missing something. It is time to pause and reflect.

And we have helped many lawyers like you with these exact problems. We will tell you how. Just hold on a little bit more.

 

 

What a high-growth small law firm or independent law practice looks like

 

Financial freedom

The legal profession is a very profitable one. You have eliminated low margin work and unreasonable clients that exhaust you. You do not take up work where financials are not justified.

Your income is growing by leaps and bounds month on month. You can have the lifestyle you want to have. Your income far outstrips your expenses and you are able to invest most of your income. 

 

Work-life balance and peace of mind

Freedom from the crazy work schedule and backbreaking work pressure, you work at your pleasure. You have total control over your time. Thanks to a great team behind you, you choose when you want to work and when you want to take a break.

 

Secure pipeline of clients and new work

There is a strong pipeline of work. You have regular client development activities planned and the machinery you have built ensures a steady flow of work. 

 

Growing brand name and reputation

You have built a strong brand in your area of work. Your clients talk about you positively to other potential clients and recommend you. The market considers you to be a premium service provider. 

You regularly write articles, blog posts, appear on interviews, webinars and TV debates, your social media is highly engaging and clients follow you to receive regular updates about your area of expertise. 

You are considered a leading authority, thought leader and influencer in your area of practice. People look up to you for innovative solutions, new ideas and predictions.

Talented young lawyers seek you out for an opportunity to work with you and learn from you. You have no difficulty in hiring. You are not afraid that talent may leave.

You are able to pay your lawyers really well. You reward high performers. You have a terrific work culture and even lawyers who leave once after being poached by top law firms want to come back very soon. High-quality lawyers are leaving jobs with big-name places to join you and work with you.  

Feels great to even imagine this picture, doesn’t it? This is what your future looks like, as a small law firm owner or an independent practitioner.
 
 

What is stopping you from getting there?

Here are the top 5 challenges for small law firm owners and independent practitioners:

 

Ad hoc approach to client acquisition and learning

Waiting to get the work before learning new skills. Asking the clients directly for work without taking the initiative to build and showcase your work. Waiting for an advance before doing your research and preparation. 

 

Knowledge and skill gap in service delivery

Law is a profession where clients want to hire the best that they can afford. If you are a cheap lawyer but your skills are of a lower order it does not help much, but if you are highly knowledgeable, and you do the best work that is available in the market, that is much easier to market. What are you doing to get there fast? Do you have a strategy for this?

 

Not investing in your own growth

You cannot expect to learn by just doing the work that you normally do over a period of time. The legal services market is evolving very fast. You need to identify new areas and upskill fast, without waiting for years to work under the guidance of a senior, acquire a post-graduate degree or prior experience at a marque law firm. If you have identified that you need help for your growth as a lawyer but do nothing about it, you cannot grow by accident. If you are not specifically investing in your own growth as well as that of your practice, there is very little chance that it is going to happen at all.

 

Reliance on practice development advice from lawyers of earlier generations who are not in sync with today’s altered reality

Most lawyers depend on practice development advice from specific mentors who are senior in the legal profession and who have built their practice long before, in a different time and age, and in a period of 10-20 years. 

Much of that advice does not work today, because the market has completely changed.

What worked for getting a job 20 years back in a law firm, does not apply now. Interviews, job descriptions, policies of employers and processes have all changed, so has competition.

Let's ask you a couple of questions. 

First, are you willing to wait it out for as long as they did, to succeed? Or do you want to try out additional steps (over and above what your mentors suggest) to radically speed up your journey? 

Second, are you sure that the techniques which worked 10 or 20 years back will be as effective today? Have you seen them working for others around you?

I am not discounting the value of the advice of seniors - it is great to rely on their legal interpretation, understanding of the bench in a particular court and their superior knowledge of litigation or corporate work on specific matters. 

However, the practice of law is evolving so fast that you need multiple mentors to guide you in different areas of professional development. 

You can do very well with specialized training and mentors for building your law practice. You need to take learnings from other disciplines such as management, digital marketing, brand building, digital transformation and automation etc.  

 

Thinking that law practice is not a business

You might think that the practice of law is poles apart from running a business. 

Businesses can advertise and are profit-making, but lawyering is a noble profession. 

A lawyer is a champion of justice and a friend of the court. 

However, running a successful law practice has several aspects which are common to a business. 

For example, content marketing, people management, operations management, financial planning, strategy and process automation - all of these can rapidly grow your practice, if you resort to the right strategy at the right time. 

It can take many years to acquire expertise in each of these areas, but those who start early and focus on these aspects do far better than those who resist this idea. 

Every single skill you learn in this regard will grow your practice and make it more stable to that extent. What you learn, you will be able to transmit to your team and build systems accordingly.

You do not have to depend on pure luck, or have grey hair or be a second or third-generation lawyer to be recognized in the industry and run a flourishing and profitable law firm or practice. 
 
The roadmap to build a successful law practice or a law firm is not a mystery. 

Here are the 5 steps necessary for any lawyer to build a profitable practice:

 

Step 1: Learn how to solve a client’s problem, i.e. acquire specific technical skills which the market needs.

The legal industry is evolving very fast - a client frequently approaches a small law firm owner or an independent practitioner for services straddling a combination of practice areas. 

For example, advice on a fintech contract may require knowledge of technology laws, banking regulations, data protection, contract drafting, negotiation and dispute resolution altogether. 

Similarly, take the example of insolvency and bankruptcy work.  For all of 2019, it was one of the most important areas of work for commercial litigators. As of 2020, after the COVID crisis, suddenly, there is a moratorium on filing cases in the NCLT under IBC for insolvency and bankruptcy. However, right now, the work that these lawyers should focus on is the restructuring of loans. There is a lot of work in this area and few lawyers who can do it.

After a year, this could very well change again. Lawyers who do not rapidly respond to the market situation are likely to struggle. 

These are just some examples - in reality, client problems pertain to many other practice area combinations.  

The challenge for a small law firm owner or an independent practitioner in these situations is to inspire the client’s confidence in his ability to handle such complex work. 

The best strategy is to choose a few niches like this (perhaps even just one) and build up a reputation as the ‘go-to lawyer’ for such work.

This kind of work can be very high margin, but several small law firms and independent lawyers fail to get such work. They stick to routine low-margin work, which is often the root of their problems.

You cannot wait to acquire prior experience or have years of expertise in these areas - you have to acquire the competence rapidly through your own resources. 

Otherwise, by the time you learn enough about an area of work, it may fall out of favour or may become already too overcrowded to start out, or the trend itself may alter in a way that it makes no sense to focus on it. 

Speed and ability to adapt to changes in the market, therefore, is key to the success of the lawyers of the new generation. And this speed and adaptability come from the ability to learn the trade rapidly rather than slowly through trial and error and observation. 

The way lawyers used to learn a skill, and practice the same thing over their entire life, looks like a luxury today. Sometimes available, but we need to learn to live without it.

  • What career benefits can you expect after pursuing this introductory program?

Why should you bother to learn about consumer litigation?

Why should you bother to learn about consumer litigation?

  • Are you a consumer? You can handle your own consumer litigation, and get justice. We will show you how to go about it.
  • Are you a lawyer? In post-covid post-lockdown world, consumer litigation will go through the roof. Airlines, hotels, educational institutes, e-commerce - a lot of businesses have been defaulting on their legal obligations, and there will be deficiency in services. Consumers will have to go to consumer court to get reparation. 
  • If you can already handle consumer litigation, great. If you need a crash course on it, here we have it for you.
  • Are you a law student? Consumer litigation is better than mooting to develop real life legal skills, and also to earn some pocket money by helping out common people, startups and SMEs with their difficult consumer disputes.
  • Want to explore beyond the world of moot courts and experience real-world litigation through consumer litigation? Do you want to practice real drafting and argue before judges? We will show you how you can do it.

Common misconceptions about consumer litigation

Common misconceptions about consumer litigation

  • There is no money in it. This is not correct. Many companies are spending a lot of money on this. 
  • The fee paid by individual litigants is very low as matters involve small sums. Even individuals who file these consumer cases are happy to pay a reasonable fee. You can build a thriving practice if you accept small fees from a large volume of clients looking for a solution to their consumer disputes.
  • There is no growth if you practice consumer law. This is not correct. Getting consumer cases from big companies is fairly easy. As you build relationships with in-house counsels and they get to see your skills and professional approach to matters, they will slowly open up to the idea of giving you other matters as well.
  • Only lawyers can argue before consumer courts, law students can’t do anything here.  In reality this is one court where law students can argue if they are authorised by a client through a special power of attorney, both in district forums and in appeals. For that matter, anyone can obtain an authorisation from a client in consumer matters and appear on behalf of another person. There is no restriction on your appearing before consumer courts. 
  • Big matters are only before the National Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission. Indeed there are some large matters of consumer disputes

This is relevant for you if you can identify with a few of the following questions:

This is relevant for you if you can identify with a few of the following questions:

  • Do you want quick wins in terms of both client acquisition and bolstering your earnings as a lawyer in the very short term?
  • Do you want to learn more about an area of practice that is not competitive at all and have a lot of opportunities?
  • Do you want to build a career in litigation in the post-COVID post-lockdown world?
  • Do you want to rapidly acquire some corporate clients and begin to build deeper relationships with them?
  • Do you want to develop your ‘court craft’ and secure opportunities to argue before judges?
  • Do you want to experience the joy of helping common people win legal battles against big corporates? 
  • Do you want to create your first set of clients in a non-competitive area of work, build a thriving practice with a large volume of matters and later grow into newer practice areas through the same clients?
  • Do you want to develop the legal knowledge and prowess to help clients solve real problems even before you graduate? 
  • Do you want to learn how to draft documents like legal notices, responses, consumer complaints and appeals, and actually get the experience of doing these things in real life?

What do your clients desire?

What do your clients desire?

  • There are consumer disputes of varied sizes. The very small ones that involve money below INR 20,000 often makes little sense to pursue given the work involved in getting a relief. Lawyers also often do not want to take up such matters as their fee expectations from such matters are very low.
  • However, for young lawyers looking to get their initial break and some experience such matters provide great opportunity to learn work, help people, build some reputation and even earn some small sums. 
  • On the other hand, corporate clients facing consumer litigation also want reliable lawyers at a reasonable rate and do not look for very senior lawyers. They are willing to give a chance to smaller lawyers in such matters. 
  • There are also consumer disputes involving large sums - non-delivery of property by builders or defective buildings, faulty medical devices or implants, expensive cars sold with defects, insurance and banking services, luxury goods, highly priced electronic goods, mobiles and laptops, ecommerce involving large ticket items, travel - which can run into amounts that are over 10 lakh - 1 crore+. In such matters clients want lawyers with proven track record and experience of handling similar matters.  
  • Many consumer cases are filed out of spite and anger, and the consumers are essentially looking for justice or some sort of retribution. Many medical negligence cases filed in consumer courts are often of this nature, where the litigant is not seeking compensation as much as he is seeking that the other side should face some serious consequence. 
  • Most of the time all the clients in this market, and much unlike other legal markets, just want that their case is being diligently pursued and that there is a reasonable cost to all of these.

What career benefits can you expect after pursuing this introductory program?

What career benefits can you expect after pursuing this introductory program? 

As a competent consumer lawyer with a reasonable volume of clients, how much can you earn by exclusively working at district level consumer courts?

 

Let us assume that the average amount of compensation per consumer dispute which is claimed by a client is INR 20,000 to INR 100,000. 

 

If the dispute is of an even lower value, we are assuming that the client will want to do the matter himself or herself, although sometimes they may come to a lawyer even for this.

 

Let us now look at a broad breakdown of what you can charge: 

  • - Drafting and filing: INR 2000-3000 per draft 
  • - Per appearance charges: INR 1000 per appearance

 

*Assume that out of pocket expenses are additional.

 

Note that we are assuming a very modest fee here. It is rare that any lawyer will charge such a low fee. However, we are assuming that being a beginner your charges will be very affordable. Let us see on this basis what could be your income potential in a month.

 

Please note that before we proceed that in high stakes matters where there is a claim against an insurer, builder or a hospital in a medical negligence case, you may be able to charge far more.

 

In order for you to appear for the maximum number of matters, they must all be filed at the same district forum. So you will have to narrowly focus on one area. 

 

Let us assume that you can represent clients for 5 matters on one day. Assume that you perform 2 new filings every week and are present for oral hearings on two days of the week.  

 

How much does that work out to?

 

Let’s do the math.

 

Aggregate monthly billing from drafting and filing work: INR 2000 x 2 drafts per week x 4 weeks: INR 16,000 

 

Aggregate monthly billing from hearings: INR 1,000 x 10 hearings per week x 4 weeks: INR 40,000

 

Total monthly billing from consumer matters: INR 56,000/- per month

 

Thus, with 10 appearances every week and 2 new matters filed every week, it is possible to earn upto INR 56,000 per month! 

 

Not too bad for a lawyer starting out on his own. 

 

What is even better is that this requires you to spend only very limited hours in court! You are free on the remaining days of the week to pursue other matters and earn more.

 

It is also important to note that consumer cases usually do not require extensive drafting and long drawn out arguments and cross examination unlike most other litigations. That means you will probably spend less time on such matters while drafting and arguing.

 

There is also a possibility of proceedings going fully online. Given that the Supreme Court, High Court and other forums and arbitral institutes are gradually shifting to online proceedings, consumer forums may follow suit as well. 

 

If that happens, you may be able to represent a consumer before district forums in multiple districts, and before the state or national commission and at a district forum, even if you are not in a location where the state commission or the national commission bench is situated. 

 

Now, you may not have so many matters to work on in your first month, but if you set out to do this dedicatedly, and do your marketing right, you can build a very reasonable practice around consumer litigation in a few months. It may not make you filthy rich, but with some time and good work, you can hope to earn as much as an associate in a good law firm!

 

What if you are unable to even take out 2 days of the week to work on your own matters and be in district forums? 

 

It may be that you do not have the time to build a full-blown consumer litigation practice. You may be working very hard under a senior and may have very little time to work on your own client development and independent matters. 

 

Still, note that the monetary return as compared to the time investment is quite high. 

 

Can you work on enough matters to earn a supplementary extra income of INR 20,000 per month, in addition to what you already work on? Would that be a worthwhile pursuit? 

 

You can use the skills acquired through this introductory program in the following ways:

 

If you practice independently, you can obtain retainer arrangements from consumer facing companies operating in the above sectors 

 

If you work under a senior, you can help consumers with disputes independently, earn a supplementary income and also increase your confidence 

 

You can prepare for in-house positions in consumer-facing companies as consumer cases represent a huge aspect of their legal work. 

Four steps through which you can become a battle-ready consumer warrior

Four steps through which you can become a battle-ready consumer warrior

Learn battle tested strategies along with sample templates on how to perform real consumer litigation work


There is a lot of information available online for free - bare acts, case laws and articles on different legal issues under the Consumer Protection Act. However, such information is not adequate to work for a real client. 

One needs practical ‘how to’ guides, strategic inputs and adequate briefing to perform specific legal tasks, along with templates and guidance on how to customize them for real client matters. You can ask any doubts on our learning management system. 


Attend live online classes to interact with practitioners, get briefed on how to perform real work and ask doubts 


There is no substitute for face-to-face learning from real interactions with practitioners who have worked on client matters. Attend 5 hours of live sessions to learn how to perform the work step-by-step. Interact with experts and ask questions to cement your learning. You can watch the recordings later also if you miss any part or need to revisit something. Acces will remain with you for 1 year. 


Develop confidence by performing practical drafting exercises and application of skills to life-like situations 


What you have learned in theory may not be of any value unless you can put it to use reliably. For this, practice in simulated scenarios is important. 

Airline pilots perform on-ground flight simulations, martial artists develop strength through practice on punching bags and mock fights, and cricketers practice in the nets to improve. 

Similarly, in our courses, you get the opportunity to apply your learning to simulated drafting and strategy assignments. 


Improve through personalized feedback and corrections from evaluators 


One cannot always see one’s own blind spots. The best athletes, CEOs, and professionals need coaches to improve their game and take it to the next level. 
 
What if you could receive line-by-line corrections and feedback on your drafts from a trained evaluator? Would it help you to improve and perform better next time?    
 
Every learner has the opportunity to get corrections and line-by-line feedback on every assignment submitted. This is a very personalized method of feedback.
 
Our students have cited this facility to be the most beneficial for their skill development. 

Training Methodology

Training Methodology

  • Access to study materials with templates through our online learning management system (LMS), Android and iOS app (access will remain active for 12 months)
  • One 3-hour and one 2-hour live class will be held (recordings available to those who miss the class) 
  • Classes will be held over 2 consecutive days from 7-10 pm on day 1 and 7-9 pm on day 2
  • You can ask questions, share your screen, get personal feedback in class 
  • Practical drafting exercises for key documents
  • Group feedback in classroom and in-line evaluator feedback 
  • You can ask questions, get your doubts cleared live as well as through the discussion board on our learning management system

List of Weekly Exercises 

Day 1: Initiation of a consumer dispute by Complainant (Representation for Complainant)

Exercise 1: How to draft a legal notice.

Exercise 2: How to draft a complaint. Draft a notice for initiation of consumer proceedings

Exercise 1: How to draft a reply notice.

Exercise 2: How to draft a version/ affidavit in evidence.

Who is this for?

Law students
Young lawyers who are interested in working with law firms

Is your motivation for working with a law firm any of the following?

Getting paid a handsome salary while working at a top brand name law firm
Getting exposure to top-notch legal work, learning how legal work is done at the top of the profession
Getting the opportunity to learn, working on high profile matters, and growing fast in your career

What are the challenges you are facing while trying to get a job in a law firm?

  • Law schools have no clear curriculum or training program on how one can get through to a law firm job. This means law students and young lawyers have to figure out what to do and how to do it on their own.
  • Some law colleges allow their students to do unlimited internships around the year, while others do not give enough internship breaks. Stringent attendance regulations at most colleges ensure that students lose a lot of opportunities and operate with a big handicap.
  • Lawyers and law students apply for law firm jobs and often get no response. They have no idea what they can do differently to evoke a response.
  • It appears to some law students and young lawyers that only the students and graduates of a few law schools get all the opportunities, and others are not even considered. 
  • Sometimes it seems that only those with personal relationships or recommendations from high places can manage to get into these big law firms.
  • If I am already working as a junior lawyer in a local court, is there anything I can do to get into a good law firm in the future? My friends say that it is not possible!
  • Law firms are always looking for experienced lawyers and not willing to give a chance to those who have no experience.
  • Law firms seem to be biased towards NLUs/5-year law courses!
  • When I got an internship, I was given pointless and meaningless clerical work. How can I make a good impression unless I am given good work where I can show my mettle?
  • I did an assessment internship with a lot of hope and did not get a job despite good feedback because there is no vacancy!
  • Law firms, while hiring in disputes, expect you to have good knowledge of drafting and court procedures, but nobody is willing to teach these during internships! Where can I learn these things?
  • My friends are doing CS, and they say it is necessary to get that qualification to get an opportunity in corporate law. Is this true?
  • Some law firms pay so little to juniors that they have to go and look for other options. How can we get a job in law firms that pay a decent salary?
  • How do I know which law firms are actually looking to hire and which ones are just looking for interns to do grunt work and will not give an opportunity to get hired later on?
  • Law firms want to hire law students who spend at least 6 months interning first. But law students do not get enough breaks from college. Law graduates find it hard to sustain themselves on a small internship stipend for 6 months.
  • There is no clear and step-by-step way to prepare for a job in a law firm, including CV building, application and interview stages. Can someone tell me what to do?
  • What kind of CV do I need to have in order to get a law firm job? Do I need to win moots, top in the class, get a CS qualification or write articles to be considered in a law firm?
  • It is so expensive to do internships! Going to a big city, finding accommodation, affording it all can be a big challenge for a law student or even a young lawyer from a smaller city. How can they get a break in a good law firm given their resource crunch?
  • Despite spending tons of money on college fees, law graduates often do not get a job that even pays their basic living expenses, and those who studied on education loan are unable to make the EMI payments!

 

Some common myths about how to get a law firm job

  • Only toppers in law schools can get jobs in top law firms.
  • You need to be a mooter if you want to get a corporate law firm job.
  • Publishing articles in journals and paper presentations in conferences is the best way to showcase practical skills for a law firm job. 
  • Law firms are only for corporate lawyers; those who want to work on disputes and litigations cannot work in a law firm.
  • To get a law firm job, LLB alone is not enough. You need to also do CS or LLM. 
  • Real learning and exposure are possible only from internships. 
  • Seniors at law firms will mentor and train us in internships.  
  • Having a long list of internships in prestigious firms will enable me to secure my dream job eventually. 
  • Only NLU students have access to the best job opportunities.
  • As a first-generation lawyer, I am seriously disadvantaged. 2nd and 3rd generation lawyers will always do better than I ever can.  
  • The placement committee of my law school will help me to get a job. They promised at the time of admission after all.
  • Doing cheap online courses and getting many certificates will ensure I get a law firm job.
  • If I do not get through to one of the big and famous law firms, it is not worth working with the smaller law firms.
  • If I do not get a law firm job as a fresher, then I have no hope of getting a top law firm job later.
  • All law firms are equal. Just get into any firm.
  • All law firms pay great salaries.

Common questions asked by law students and young lawyers interested in working with law firms

Common questions asked by law students and young lawyers interested in working with law firms

  • I do not know my area of interest. How to find out what I should work in?
  • Should I specialize so early in my career? Will that increase my chances or decrease opportunity?
  • Which law firms should I apply for, given my interests, skills and prior experience? 
  • I want to secure a law firm job. How should I go about the entire process? What should I do next? 
  • I am not from an NLU. How can I still get access to the best law firm jobs which NLU students get?
  • I am a first-generation lawyer and do not have contacts in law firms. Can I get a good law firm job or internships?  
  • I have applied to a few good law firms and am waiting for a response. What else can I do?
  • I am not getting enough work or guidance in my internship. What can I do to get more work, contribute more to my seniors, maximise my learning and increase my chances of getting a law firm job?     
  • Where should I intern? What can I do to maximise my chance of converting my internship into a PPO (pre-placement offer)?
  • How can I approach law firms to understand what I need to do in order to get a job?

Have you tried these things before but nothing worked?

  • Applying to lots of law firms, sending emails and consistently calling them up to see if you can get an internship
  • Applied to a lot of vacancies in law firms that you saw on Linkedin or any other portal
  • Attended career fairs hoping to find a job
  • Paid a lot of money to professional CV drafting services to draft the perfect CV and cover letter
  • I went for many internships but only to be not offered any job nor called back for another internship at the end.
  • Tried to get recommendations from seniors, family friends or other people to get a job in a law firm only to be disappointed in the end despite such recommendations

 

Why do you think things have not worked for you so far?

  • Consider that there are some shortcomings regarding how you have approached the entire problem.
  • Most people think that it is an access problem. Access can be created. But if you get access, are you ready to capitalise on that opportunity?
  • Have you figured out what will make you stand out from other law students or lawyers also interning or interviewing with the firm? If not, you can work very hard to get access to the opportunity, but you will not be able to convert it.
  • Note that a large number of lawyers get fired from their law firm jobs within the first 3-6 months. Many quit on their own. Even if you get a job when you are not prepared, you will not succeed in either keeping your job or excelling at it. 
  • There are 3 major steps you need to figure out. The first step is to learn the work that associates do in a law firm for the area of practice in which you want to work. 
  • The second step is to build a CV and track record that helps you to get that internship or interview where you can showcase that knowledge. 
  • And the third step is to close the deal through your outstanding performance in the interview or the assessment internship once you get that opportunity.
  • Preparation, preparation, preparation. Preparation can help you to beat all other odds, such as not being from a non-brand name law college, not receiving good marks in law college, or even not knowing anyone who can recommend you.
  • When I was in law school, I needed recommendations for getting certain internships. I was always able to obtain them from my professional network, as my parents or family could never help me anyway. 
  • We need to build our own professional network so that we can reach the opportunities we seek. You need to build your professional network, too, starting right away.
  • If something has not worked for you, it is probably because you need to follow a different approach. And perhaps, you need to work a lot harder, but with a precise focus.
  • Having helped a lot of law students from all kind of backgrounds to get law firm jobs even at tier 1 law firms, I can assure you that nothing is out of reach. You just need to work strategically and consistently. Some of you can do it in 3 months, and others may need 2 years, but if you work for it, it is not unachievable.
  • It is most competitive and difficult to get into a big law firm at a fresher level. Thereafter, it gets easier and easier, if you have the right skills, to get a job in a big or small law firm.

Five steps to be ‘law-firm ready’ irrespective of your grades, law school, work experience or any other limitation of your past

Step 1 - Learn about the expectation at a law firm from a young lawyer and identify the gap between where you are and where you need to be

The first step requires you to identify the different types of law firms and the work they perform, the types of solutions provided to clients, the skills required to work in a law firm and the expectations from an associate. 

You cannot prepare for all of them, but we train our students to learn the work and skillset of an associate with 2 years of experience. At the entry level, if you have that much skill, you will easily stand out, and law firms will find you to be an excellent hire. 

You need to identify the gap between where you need to be and where you stand currently. This is the starting point. 

 

Step 2 - Focused preparation to acquire sector-specific skills that you can demonstrate in your CV, applications and interviews

The next step is to start learning the skills which you need to acquire, one at a time. 

For instance, if you want to work in a law firm in the M&A and investment team, you need to learn about  deal structuring, due diligence, drafting of SHA and SSA and other relevant agreements, learn how negotiations take place, deal compliance, and various regulations that govern these deals. Out of these things, you can specifically learn the things that junior lawyers are expected to do, such as filing specific forms with the RBI, managing the data room, preparing due diligence questionnaires and requisition lists, writing due diligence reports and so on.

On the other hand, if you want to get a role in an arbitration or disputes team, you have to learn very different skills. For instance, you should learn how to draft litigation and arbitration related documents and have a great grasp of procedural laws. 

To succeed in this stage, you have to proceed in a highly focussed direction, in comparison to your peers who will probably do more general things based on the wisdom of the masses - such as read pink newspapers or read textbooks on company law! None of that is bad, but probably not enough to see them through to their end goals.

You are free to acquire these essential skills on your own or take up a course with us to accelerate your journey. 

At this stage, you will see that the world is flat for all young lawyers and that every law firm opportunity is accessible and within your reach, provided you can demonstrate that you will be a highly productive young associate once hired and not spend a lot of time trying to learn the basics.  

 

Step 3 - Build up a track record and showcase your work to stand out.

After you have acquired the skills necessary to work in a law firm in the sector in which you are interested, it is time to demonstrate what you know to the public. You need to have people who know about your interest and commitment to learning more about the area of work you have chosen and the effort you have put into that direction through consistent pursuit. 
 
How can you demonstrate all these things?

There are plenty of methods to accomplish this. Writing blog posts and articles, attending or organizing events or webinars, creating youtube videos or podcasts, doing internships, helping startups or other entities in need of help and pro bono legal support, running helplines - there are a lot of things one can do in order to build up such track record.

You may choose what works best for you based on your talents and proclivities.

You can publish practice-area specific articles, create explainer videos of the problems faced by clients in these areas and even perform real work for startups and people who need legal help. You can file PILs or work with NGOs and voluntary organizations, or even business associations to help them with their legal needs.

This is the best way to build up a stellar CV and even a professional network that you can count on.

Let’s say that I want to land a competition law job. What should I be doing here?

I should try to go for competition law events and moots, even as a volunteer if not as a participant, go for competition law specific internships, work as a research assistant for competition lawyers and professors who specialise in this area of law, organize or volunteer in an event related to competition law, present papers in the subject, write articles and blog posts about it, or even start a podcast where you invite competition lawyers and interview them!

What if you just write an analysis on 50 most important competition law judgments by COMPAT? How many competition lawyers will probably read it?

There is a whole lot you can do to create a track record and demonstrate a sustained interest in the area, and it goes a long way to bag you amazing opportunities. 

 

Step 4 - Share your work, reach out to mentors and build long-term relationships.

This is the part where you create deep and meaningful relationships in the legal industry that will help you to bag jobs, internships and even client opportunities.

While most young lawyers are dependent on one senior to mentor and train them, you will have the opportunity of reaching out to hundreds of seniors and selecting your mentors. 

Most junior lawyers have one-way communication with seniors, where they are asking for a job or internship and following up on this communication after not receiving a response.

In comparison, you can share your work for feedback, actively interact with lawyers on social media and start richer, deeper and more long-term relationships and add value. 

Your interactions will be rich and covering a wide range of topics. You may receive insights about the industry in informal conversations that your peers will have no idea about. 

You can also learn to use tools like informational interviews to learn more about various areas of practice and find mentors who can help you.

Networking and having people who will vouch for you and who refer you to opportunities increases your chances by manifold.

 

Step 5 - Preparation for an internship, PPO interviews & job interviews

Most young lawyers perform this step without any of the prior steps. This leads to their preparation being very superficial. Most are, in fact, thinking that they will go and learn from the internship itself, and they do not prepare themselves for these internships prior to joining the internship.

This results in their inability to create any significant opportunity out of the internship. 

While they know that they must be confident, they often end up nervous in internships or interviews, wait passively for work to be delegated, or questions to be asked by the interviewer. This is primarily because they do not know what to expect next. This is not how top performers function.   

In the case of LawSikho students, 90 percent of your job preparation is actually complete by the time you arrive at this stage. 

If you prepare as per the method explained above, your CV will stand out, your job and internship emails will be compelling and opened by the recruiter, your follow-up efforts will be effective, and you will get responses. You will also have good lawyers willing to put in a word or even vouch for you with their friends and colleagues.

Your interview will also give a very different impression to the recruiter in comparison to other young lawyers. 

In order to ensure that you are fully prepared, you should practice a few mock interviews.

 

Bonus: Step 6 -> How to excel at your job once you get it and get the maximum bonus

Getting a job is just the start. Next comes the hard part, performing every day so you can actually succeed as a lawyer. Law firms are notorious for firing people who do not manage to perform within the first 3-6 months. 

You may have heard of the legendary work pressure, long hours and stress.

This happens because most law graduates who join law firms are very underprepared for the work they have to do. 

What do they end up doing?

 

  • Make a lot of mistakes owing to lack of knowledge and skills - leading to loss of reputation and face before their team and bosses.
  • Fail to effectively communicate with their seniors because they do not know what questions to ask or when they need to raise an alarm 
  • They take a lot of time to turn in work, or they do it quickly but get it very wrong.
  • They have to redo their work again and again due to mistakes and rejections
  • They fail to get a good bonus, and often are overlooked for promotions, and sometimes actively encouraged to leave the firm
  • If nothing else, the stress of being scolded repeatedly, loss of dignity and self-confidence due to making frequent errors, and the pressure of learning the work while they are on the clock take a toll on them, and they often quit on their own

 

You need to learn several skills to avoid this situation. There are hard legal skills you should know, but there are many soft skills you need as well.

Research, communication, time management, how to handle multiple deadlines, how to organise your work, how to take feedback from seniors, how to find out the gap between what you want and what your boss wants - there is a lot to learn. 

If you perform well on the other hand, which we teach our students to do, you can, in fact, get a higher bonus than your peers and get promoted within the firm much faster.

 

What is the solution to all these problems?

It will take a while if you want to learn and implement the solutions to all these problems. I assure you that we cannot teach all these in a 5-hour workshop; rather, it takes about a year of hard work from your side and ours, in most cases.

We have been training lawyers and law students to get through law firms and not only that but excel in their work for many years now. 

We have helped hundreds of lawyers to build stable law firm careers.

Who is this for?

Law students looking for a career in commercial disputes, corporate litigation, banking and finance laws
Lawyers who want to work at law firms in commercial disputes and corporate litigation teams or as in-house counsel with banks or NBFCs.
Independent lawyers looking to get recovery work from banks, NBFCs and fintech companies.
In-house counsels who frequently deal with cheque and NACH mandate bouncing cases.

Why is it necessary to learn about cheque bounce cases?

  • Are you a lawyer? While cheque bounce work has always been an easy way to get  independent clients, in the post-covid post-lockdown world, payment defaults and cheque bounces will increase further as businesses face liquidity issues and a massive recession. 
  • There is a tremendous increase in cheque as well as NACH default matters. Corporate and individual clients need legal assistance in dealing with these. There will be increased demand for lawyers who can work on these matters.   
  • Are you a law student? Do you want to build a career in litigation or work in a litigation firm, or with a senior? Are you finding it difficult to obtain internships? Cheque dishonour work can be quickly learnt by you to prove your mettle. 
  • Electronic payments are not excluded - ECS/ NACH payments are covered by the same laws as that of cheque bounce. Learning how to deal with these defaults will increase your employability as well as appeal to potential clients.    
  • What about the post dated cheques (PDCs) that you give for quite a few payments - what can you do if there’s a slippage in maintaining the balance, your cheque bounces and you receive a notice for payment? How would you draft a reply?
  • These are very lucrative matters because if you are able to recover payments, clients are very happy to remunerate you for your efforts. Many small law firms and independent lawyers are able to build a practice rapidly around this kind of work.
  • Cheque bounce litigation work is a ‘gateway service’ for a lawyer - it enables a lawyer to put a ‘foot in the door’, while dealing with new clients. If you show some initial results, a client will be happy to give you more complex and high-value work. 

 

Some things you’re thinking about cheque bounce cases which are not true

  • There will not be many cases to work on, because most people are using net-banking these days. Okay, how about the PDCs you give for some of your loan repayments? Or your society maintenance payments? What if you’re a lawyer advising a society? Cheques are the most common form of security provided these days, and cheque bounce cases are dozen a dime. Also, NACH mandate (electronic payment such as ECS) bouncing is treated in the same way as a cheque bounce and can be prosecuted in the same way.
  • The work is low-paying, and one needs to rely on volumes. Not if you’re dealing with high value cheques - like payments towards under construction properties or multiple cheques given as security for loan repayment. 
  • The work is relatively ‘easy’ and there is not much scope for value addition to clients. This is a mistaken belief - in any cheque bounce case, there is a risk of non-bailable warrants being issued and arrest of directors. The complainant is looking for a quick settlement from the defendant owing to threat of arrest of the defendant’s directors, while the defendant is looking to avoid arrest, delay proceedings or question the debt itself. The work is outcome-oriented and clients are interested in engaging lawyers who can provide results. This requires lawyers from both sides, that is, the complainant or the defendant’s side, to handle the matter skilfully. An untrained lawyer is prone to making mistakes which delays the outcome or heavily costs the client. 
  • Competition for working on cheque bounce cases is very high - I cannot charge much and have to keep my fees low to get clients, which is unsustainable. There is a lack of skilled lawyers in the market and if you provide quick results, you can be remunerated for your time and earn reasonable margins. Further, as this is a gateway service, a satisfied client will give you more complex and high-paying work. 

If you’re good with Section 138 matters, what is the kind of work that you can get?

Primarily, you will get work-related to cheque dishonour and ECS/ NACH (i.e. electronic payment dishonour). The work can be of the following kinds

 

  • Pre-litigation advisory work from startups and small businesses on recovery-related matters. 
  • Litigation briefs from independent clients (suppliers or defaulters). 
  • Retainers from banks, financial institutions and other companies to work on cheque bounce cases on a volume-basis in a specific court.

 

If you are working for the complainant’s side your objective is to secure arrest or settlement. If you are working for the defendant’s side your objective is to avoid arrest through various strategies or settle the dispute at a lower point.  

As you handle these matters, you will also keep an eye on adding more skillsets and taking up different and more high-margin work from existing clients as they are satisfied with your results.  

If you’re able to recover the funds that the founder is so desperately looking for, you will be the go-to person for him for other matters as well. This is a gateway service for many other legal matters, especially lucrative commercial litigation.

 

Who are likely to be your clients?

  • Suppliers: Often in cases where a business has defaulted in payments to one supplier, they have done so for others too. You may be able to secure matters from many unpaid suppliers of the same delinquent customer. Once you produce results for one client, they will refer many others to you, given the nature of the work. 
  • Banks, financial institutions and NBFCs: You may be able to represent financial institutions, banks or NBFCs which take cheques as a security against amounts lent. These are likely to have multiple cases of default and even if you are able to represent one such bank, NBFC or financial institution, you can earn a significant amount without having to spend a lot of time and effort in looking for further clients. 
  • Large manufacturing companies: Similarly, large manufacturing corporate entities which provide goods and services and which accept payments through cheques or accept payments on credit (on the security of post-dated cheques) will have many such matters.
  • Startups and SMEs: Sometimes, smaller entities which have a lower negotiating power cannot dictate the mode of payments and may have to accept payments in the form of post dated cheques. Such funds may also be very crucial for such small businesses.

 

What do your clients desire?

  • An affordable lawyer with clear understanding of the steps involved who will handle their matters diligently and competently. 
  • This is one area of work where you do not have to grow grey hair before clients entrust their work to you. 
  • Many clients have a lot of work and they are willing to try out new lawyers because they can’t overburden one lawyer with too many matters in the fear that the performance may drop due to too many matters being given to one lawyer.
  • Also, given that cases may have to be filed in different places all over the country, even if you are from smaller cities or districts you can get enough work (jurisdiction is where the cheque is presented to a bank branch). This means in-house counsels are looking for lawyers who can help with these matters in many different places and can’t send all work to lawyers in a single city.
  • Clients also want regular updates, information about how the matter is progressing and diligent processing of the matters. 
  • You will get many matters from outstation clients who are worried about getting arrested due to cheque bounce matters and you will basically have to represent them to get a settlement done and close out a matter. 

 

What kind of fees can you expect while dealing with a Section 138 matter 

Even as someone who has recently taken up practice, this is one area you can pick up and expect to earn INR 5000 to INR 10000 for drafting a legal notice for dishonour of cheque depending on the client, place of filing a case and the recoverable at stake. 

For filing a complaint you can expect to earn further INR 10000-15000 and even further fees for attending a hearing depending upon the state you are in. In all, you can expect to earn INR 50000 over the course of the proceedings if the recoverable is north of 5 lakhs, which is a pretty decent amount for someone in the initial stages of practice to get from one specific matter. 

If the recoverable is of a lesser amount, clients may not be willing to pay this much per matter. 

However, if you are handling multiple matters from the same client such as a bank or NBFC, you may be able to earn a good amount simply on the basis of the number of matters.

In this kind of work, you should definitely target a volume of work because large volumes create efficiency and economy of scale as matters often have very similar facts. 

Though you will have to be aware of exactly how to draft the notice and complaint and pay attention to the timelines, and act in a very precise manner with great diligence, these matters are neither laborious nor time consuming. Compared to a standard civil litigation or writ petition matter, drafting, research work, number of hearings and arguments involved in a cheque bounce case would likely be far lesser.

This ensures higher margin for you as you can do more matters. 

You can also get monthly retainership from businesses having many cheque bounce cases in the same court.

You need to be able to know what you need to include in the notice and how to ensure that it is delivered appropriately so that you have adequate evidence for everything. You must know every single document that you need to attach to the complaint.

Airline pilots perform on-ground flight simulations, martial artists develop strength through practice on punching bags and mock fights, and cricketers practice in the nets to improve.

One cannot always see one’s own blind spots. The best athletes, CEOs, and professionals need coaches to improve their game and take it to the next level.

Who is this for
